newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Swine fever seen cutting Europe's feed demand.
newsitem.headline: Swine fever seen cutting Europe's feed demand.

text.p: Fears over the impact swine fever will have on animal feed demand in the Netherlands is bolstering the view that prices for some products will ease in the coming months, traders and analysts said on Monday.

"People are talking about a 25 to 30 percent reduction in demand for hogfeed. It's not having a big effect yet but it will from the end of this month," said analyst Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.

The swine fever outbreak has now spread to around 220 farms in the south of the country, and has prompted the destruction of two million pigs. Dutch Farm Minister Jozias van Aartsen said last week the final number of cases may reach 300.
Traders said the impact on demand was making compounders wary of taking distant positions.
Products affected will include citruspulp pellets, which although not in plentiful supply at the moment, should be arriving in greater quantities from next month.
"The Brazilian crop is a record one and it will be coming earlier than usual," Van Dijk said, predicting heavy arrivals in north-west Europe from July onwards.
Tapioca may also be affected, particularly as arrivals are expected to swell in the second half of this month.
"With old crop grain prices coming down, I wonder if tapioca prices can hold up," he added.
In the very near-term, the strong dollar continues to dampen physical buisiness in Europe, with soymeal prices marked higher this morning after another rise in Chicago old crop futures.

But traders noted this situation may be changing after Friday's USDA strong soybean new crop export sales figure, which suggested world buyers had covered their immediate needs and had enough to tide them over until the new crop became available.

The market is also eagerly anticipating the next soybean ending stocks estimate from the USDA, due on June 12. It was surprisingly left unchanged in May at 125 million bushels after many in the market had expected it to be lowered as far as 105 million bushels.

The feeling the USDA could lower the carry-over this time, may spark increased speculative activity ahead of the release date but many are likely to be "once bitten twice shy" after trying a similar play before the May figure, traders said.

Nearby European sunmeal and rapemeal could be neglected over the next few weeks as little old crop material will be available. Crushers also take the opportunity over the next few months to do essential maintainance ahead of the new season.
"The larger rapeseed crop and good crushing margins will mean they'll want to be firing on all cylinders by September," Van Dijk commented.
